cardBlurb: You do not need twenty employees to run a real business. You need five seats filled by five A players, and most owners skip the one that compounds the most.
title: The five seats
desc: The five seats every real business needs filled, what each one owns, and the one most owners skip.
em: Five A players, not twenty employees.
lead: Owners think a real business needs twenty people. It needs five seats, each filled by one person who is excellent at that seat and nothing else. Here are the five, what each owns, and the one that compounds the most and gets skipped the most.
tiles: The five seats, what each owns, and how to tell if a seat is empty.
Map your current team onto the seats and find the gaps.
Scorecards per seat, the hiring order, and the handoffs between them.

sections.label: The five seats
sections.h2: One person, one seat, one job.
body: steps
The closer.

Brings in the money. A senior salesperson, whatever you call it. Feed them leads and be willing to overpay the market, because a good closer makes everything else in the business easier when money is always coming in.
The operator.
Delivers the work. Ops, fulfillment, service. One person who makes the thing and loves the thing, not four people each working on one part of it.
The numbers.
Books, payroll, invoicing, chasing money that is already yours. Truly important at scale, because you cannot make decisions to grow if you do not know where the money is.
The pipeline.
Marketing, content, partnerships, collaborations. Anyone getting in front of the closer so the money keeps coming in.
The GM.

The second in command, the integrator. Manages the other four and makes sure the people who are working are working together. The seat most owners skip, and the one that compounds the most over time, especially if you are the CEO.
said
The rule
You just need one A player in each of those seats. A player means the best you can find for that seat, not the most senior person you already have.

sections.label: How to spot an empty seat
sections.h2: Most businesses have five seats and two people.
body: p

An empty seat does not look empty. It looks like the owner doing it at eleven at night. The closer's seat is empty when the owner is still on every sales conversation. The numbers seat is empty when payroll is a surprise. The pipeline seat is empty when the closer has nobody to talk to on Tuesday. The GM seat is empty when every decision comes back to the owner and nothing happens while they are away.
checks
Which seat are you sitting in that someone else should own?
Which seat has two people in it, each doing half?
Which seat has nobody, and who is quietly absorbing it?
If you left for two weeks, which seat would stop?
linkedin

You do not need twenty employees. You need five seats: someone who brings in the money, someone who makes the thing, someone who owns the numbers, someone who fills the pipeline, and the person who manages the other four. Most owners skip the last one. It is the one that compounds.

sections.label: The hiring order
sections.h2: Fill the seat that is bleeding, not the one that is fun.
body: p

There is no universal order. The right next hire is the seat whose absence costs the most this quarter. A business with a full pipeline and no closer hires the closer. A business with a great closer and a chaotic delivery hires the operator. A business where the owner is the bottleneck for every decision hires the GM, even though it feels like paying someone to do what the owner already does. That is the point.
p
Before any hire, write the seat: what it owns, the one number it is measured on, and what done looks like in ninety days. A seat without a number is a title, and titles do not compound.

ws: One name per seat, or a blank.
fields: Who owns bringing in the money? Their one number?
Who makes the thing? Who owns the books, payroll, and invoicing?
Who is getting in front of the closer every week?
Who manages the other four? If it is you, what stops when you are away?
pr: Map your team onto the seats.
Paste your people and what they actually do. It finds the empty seats, the doubled seats, and the next hire.
prompt: Map my team onto the five seats: the closer (brings in the money), the operator (delivers the work), the numbers (books, payroll, invoicing, collections), the pipeline (marketing, content, partnerships, feeding the closer), and the GM (manages the other four). For each seat: 1. Who sits in it today, based only on what they actually do (not their title). "Owner" is a valid answer. "Nobody" is a valid answer. 2. The one number that seat should be measured on in my business. 3. Empty, doubled, or filled. A seat the owner sits in that someone else should own counts as empty. Then: 4. THE NEXT HIRE: which seat is costing the most this quarter and why, in three lines. 5. THE SEAT DESCRIPTION for that hire: what it owns, the one number, what done looks like at ninety days. 6. One sentence on what stops if the owner leaves for two weeks. Use only what I tell you. Never invent a person or a number. MY TEAM AND WHAT EACH PERSON ACTUALLY DOES: [paste]
